# Complement 3a receptor 1 on macrophages and Kupffer cells is not required for the pathogenesis of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease

## Authors

- Edwin A Homan<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0002-2923-9635](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-2923-9635))
- Ankit Gilani<sup>1</sup>
- Alfonso Rubio-Navarro<sup>1</sup>
- Maya A Johnson<sup>1</sup>
- Odin M Schaepkens<sup>1</sup>
- Eric Cortada<sup>1</sup>
- Renan Pereira de Lima<sup>1</sup>

## Abstract

Together with obesity and type 2 diabetes, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a growing global epidemic. Activation of the complement system and infiltration of macrophages has been linked to progression of metabolic liver disease. The role of complement receptors in macrophage activation and recruitment in MASLD remains poorly understood. In human and mouse, C3AR1 in the liver is expressed primarily in Kupffer cells, but is downregulated in humans with MASLD compared to obese controls. To test the role of complement 3a receptor (C3aR1) on macrophages and liver resident macrophages in MASLD, we generated mice deficient in C3aR1 on all macrophages (C3aR1-MφKO) or specifically in liver Kupffer cells (C3aR1-KpKO) and subjected them to a model of metabolic steatotic liver disease. We show that macrophages account for the vast majority of C3ar1 expression in the liver. Overall, C3aR1-MφKO and C3aR1-KpKO mice have similar body weight gain without significant alterations in glucose homeostasis, hepatic steatosis and fibrosis, compared to controls on a MASLD-inducing diet. This study demonstrates that C3aR1 deletion in macrophages or Kupffer cells, the predominant liver cell type expressing C3ar1, has no significant effect on liver steatosis, inflammation or fibrosis in a dietary MASLD model.

## Introduction

Obesity and related metabolic diseases such as type 2 diabetes (T2D) and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) remain a worldwide epidemic with increasing prevalence (Ge et al., 2020; Younossi et al., 2018). MASLD describes the constellation of hepatic lipid deposition, inflammation, and fibrosis associated with obesity and T2D that ultimately leads to MASH cirrhosis, which has become the leading cause of liver transplantation in the United States (Ferguson and Finck, 2021; Friedman et al., 2018; Stefan et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2021). Notably, MASLD is increasingly recognized as an important risk-enhancing factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (Duell et al., 2022; Kasper et al., 2021).

Liver macrophages help to maintain hepatic homeostasis and consist of embryo-derived resident macrophages called Kupffer cells, which self-renew and do not migrate, or peripheral monocyte-derived macrophages, which infiltrate into liver tissue upon metabolic or toxic liver injury and under certain circumstances can take on Kupffer cell-like identity (Barreby et al., 2022; Cai et al., 2019; Guilliams and Scott, 2022; Park et al., 2023; Sakai et al., 2019). In obesity, bone-marrow-derived myeloid cells migrate to the steatotic liver, and pro-inflammatory recruited macrophages are postulated to drive the progression of MASLD to MASH (Krenkel et al., 2020). Spatial proteogenomics reveals a population of lipid-associated macrophages near bile canaliculi that is induced by local lipid exposure and drives fibrosis in steatotic regions of murine and human liver (Guilliams et al., 2022). In addition, deep transcriptomic profiling in human MASLD has identified candidate gene signatures for steatohepatitis and fibrosis with possible therapeutic implications (Govaere et al., 2020).

Activation of the body’s complement system leads to increased cell lysis, phagocytosis, and inflammation (Merle et al., 2015), and it is increasingly recognized as an important contributor to regulation of metabolic disorders such as T2D and MASLD (Kolev and Kemper, 2017; Zhao et al., 2022). In human liver biopsies, higher lobular inflammation scores correlate with activation of the complement alternative pathway (Segers et al., 2014), which can signal via the C3a receptor 1 (C3aR1), a Gi-coupled G protein-coupled receptor (Markiewski and Lambris, 2007). The complement 3 polypeptide (C3) is cleaved by C3 convertase to the activated fragment, C3a, which then binds C3aR1 (Yadav et al., 2023). Complement factor D (CFD), also known as the adipokine adipsin, is the rate-limiting step in the alternative pathway of complement activation (Flier et al., 1987; Xu et al., 2001).

Several studies have reported opposing roles of adipsin and C3aR1 on hepatic steatosis in diet-induced obesity (Lim et al., 2013; Polyzos et al., 2016; Han and Zhang, 2021). Our lab has found that adipsin/CFD is critical for maintaining pancreatic beta cell mass and function (Lo et al., 2014; Gómez-Banoy et al., 2019). Murine obese and diabetic models such as db/db mice and high-fat diet (HFD) feeding result in very low circulating adipsin (Flier et al., 1987). Replenishing adipsin in db/db mice raises levels of C3a and insulin, lowers blood glucose levels, and inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis (Lo et al., 2014). However, whole-body deletion of C3aR1 decreases macrophage infiltration and activation in adipose tissue, protects from HFD-induced obesity and glucose intolerance, and decreases hepatic steatosis and inflammation (Mamane et al., 2009). In a model of fibrosing steatohepatitis, bone-marrow-derived macrophages were found to activate hepatic stellate cells, which was blunted in whole-body C3aR1 KO mice (Han et al., 2019).

In the present study, we aim to explore the macrophage-specific effect of complement receptor signaling in MASLD pathogenesis. To determine the consequences of macrophage and Kupffer cell ablation of C3aR1, we use a murine dietary model of MALFD/MASH, the Gubra Amylin Nash (GAN) diet, which has macronutrient similarities to the Western diet and produces similar histologic and transcriptomic changes to human MASLD/MASH (Boland et al., 2019; Hansen et al., 2020; Vacca et al., 2024).

## Results

### C3AR1 is expressed in human and mouse liver, primarily in Kupffer cells

In the scRNA-Seq database, Human Protein Atlas, C3AR1 is broadly expressed throughout the body, with increased abundance in tissues rich in immunologic cell types, such as bone marrow and appendix (Figure 1A; Uhlén et al., 2015). In a single-cell transcriptomic database of healthy human liver, C3AR1 expression predominates in the macrophage and Kupffer cell population, with minimal-to-undetectable C3AR1 expression in hepatocytes or hepatic stellate cells by scRNA-Seq (Figure 1B; MacParland et al., 2018). In the mouse liver scRNA-Seq database, Tabula Muris, C3ar1 is similarly expressed primarily in Kupffer cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; The Tabula Muris Consortium et al., 2018).

### Hepatic CFD and C3AR1 are downregulated in human MASLD/MASH

We also examined data from Suppli and coworkers, who performed bulk transcriptomic analysis of human liver samples from an age-matched cohort of healthy controls and obese controls without MASLD, as well as MASLD and MASH patients without cirrhosis (Suppli et al., 2019). Both CFD and C3AR1 were unchanged in obese subjects without MASLD compared to healthy controls, but both CFD and C3AR1 were significantly downregulated in liver biopsies from both MASLD and MASH patients compared to both healthy controls and obese subjects without MASLD (Figure 1C). Interestingly, both CFD and C3AR1 levels were slightly higher in MASH individuals compared to those with MASLD only.

### Murine MASH model recapitulates key features of human MASH

At 5 weeks of age, we subjected C3ar1flox/flox control mice to standard regular diet (RD) or GAN diet (Boland et al., 2019; Hansen et al., 2020). After 28 weeks of GAN diet, male mice gained body weight compared to RD (Figure 1D), primarily as fat mass (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C), but weight gain in female GAN-fed mice was attenuated. Histologic signs of MASLD were present in GAN-fed mice (Figure 1E), most notably hepatic steatosis and hepatocyte ballooning (Figure 1F), and liver fibrosis measured by collagen deposition nearly doubled with GAN compared to RD (Figure 1G). Both hepatic C3ar1 and Cfd gene expression were robustly increased on GAN compared to RD, as were markers of macrophage infiltration, hepatic inflammation, and fibrosis, including collagen gene expression, indicating progression to fibrotic MASH (Figure 1H). In female control mice on GAN diet, there were no significant differences in C3ar1 expression or other gene markers, although there was a nonsignificant trend toward increased inflammation and fibrosis compared to regular diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

### Macrophage-specific C3aR1 deletion does not alter glucose homeostasis

Owing to higher levels of C3ar1 in murine MASLD and the differential regulation of C3AR1 gene in MASLD humans, this motivated us to interrogate the role of pathophysiological role of C3ar1 in macrophages in MASLD. We generated transgenic mice with macrophage-specific deletion of C3aR1 by crossing C3ar1flox/flox mice with Lyz2Cre transgenic mice (C3aR1-MφKO) to target both liver resident macrophages and recruited monocytes. C3ar1flox/flox mice were used as controls. Successful deletion of C3ar1 in macrophages from the C3aR1-MφKO mouse was confirmed by quantitative RT-PCR of isolated peritoneal macrophages that were F4/80+and CD68+by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (Figure 2A). In liver tissue, C3ar1 expression was reduced by ~88% in both male and female C3aR1-MφKO (Figure 2B). These results indicate that macrophages account for the vast majority of C3ar1 expression in the liver.

When placed on GAN diet, there was no significant difference in weight gain between control and C3aR1-MφKO mice (Figure 2C). There was similarly no difference in percent lean or fat mass between these mice (Figure 2D). Glucose tolerance tests performed in fasted mice after 27 weeks GAN diet found no significant differences between control and C3aR1-MφKO mice (Figure 2E). There was also no difference in insulin sensitivity as measured by insulin tolerance tests in male mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). Insulin resistance as measured by comparing the ratio of fasting glucose level to fasting insulin level (HOMA-IR) was also unchanged between controls and C3aR1-MφKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). Circulating serum ALT levels were unchanged in male control and C3aR1-MφKO mice on GAN diet (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).

### Macrophage-specific C3aR1 deletion does not significantly impact hepatic steatosis or fibrosis

Liver samples collected after 28–30 weeks of GAN or regular diet did not show significant differences in liver mass between control and C3aR1-MφKO mice (Figure 2F). Male mice on GAN diet developed similar qualitative appearance on histology (Figure 2G), and slide image analysis showed similar proportions of lipid droplet area and collagen area (Figure 2H and I). This indicates that there were no significant differences in steatosis or fibrosis between GAN-fed control and C3aR1-MφKO male mice. While C3ar1 expression was markedly reduced in the C3aR1-MφKO liver tissue (Figure 2B), there were no detectable gene expression changes in markers of fibrosis, inflammation, or lipid handling on either GAN or regular diet (Figure 2J and K). Similarly, in female mice there were also no significant differences between control and C3aR1-MφKO mouse liver on either GAN or regular diet in a subset of key gene markers of fibrosis or inflammation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

### Kupffer-cell-specific C3aR1 deletion does not alter weight gain or glucose homeostasis

To explore whether there may be competing effects between recruited monocytes and liver resident macrophages (Kupffer cells), we next generated Kupffer-cell-specific C3aR1 knockout mice (C3aR1-KpKO) by crossing C3ar1flox/flox mice to Clec4f-Cre transgenic mice and fed them GAN diet. C3ar1flox/flox mice were used as controls. Body weight gain was similar between genotypes for both male and female mice (Figure 3A), and there was no difference in body composition between control and C3aR1-KpKO mice on GAN diet (Figure 3B). There was similarly no significant difference in glucose homeostasis between the genotypes during a glucose tolerance test (Figure 3C).

### Kupffer-cell-specific C3aR1 deletion does not significantly impact hepatic steatosis or fibrosis

Liver mass was not significantly different between control and C3aR1-KpKO mice on GAN diet (Figure 3D). Liver sections appeared qualitatively similar by histology stained with Masson’s trichrome (Figure 3E). There were similar levels of hepatic steatosis in these mice as measured by percent lipid droplet area (Figure 3F). When measured by collagen proportional area, there was no significant differences in liver fibrosis between C3aR1-KpKO and control mice (Figure 3G). While C3ar1 expression was reduced by 73% in liver tissue of C3aR1-KpKO mice, there were no significant differences in expression of inflammatory, fibrotic, or lipid handling gene markers (Figure 3H). C3ar1 expression similarly decreased by ~90% in liver tissue of female C3aR1-KpKO mice fed regular diet compared to control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). These data also indicate that Kupffer cells account for ~80% of hepatic C3ar1 gene expression in our mouse model of MASLD/MASH.

## Discussion

Overall, we found that macrophage or Kupffer cell expression of C3ar1 does not impact body weight gain or histologic/transcriptomic features of MASLD/MASH in a murine dietary model. Deletion of C3aR1 in the macrophage population throughout the body, or specifically in Kupffer cells, did not affect weight gain, glucose homeostasis, or extent of hepatic steatosis/fibrosis. With long term GAN diet feeding that has been previously shown to model human MASLD/MASH, we did not observe significant differences in liver abnormalities with the KO mice.

Our findings in macrophage-specific C3aR1 KO mice contrast with prior observations in whole-body C3aR1 KO mice (Mamane et al., 2009), which are protected from diet-induced obesity, have improved glucose tolerance, and exhibit decreased hepatic steatosis. In both our macrophage- and Kupffer-cell-specific C3aR1 KO mice, which had similar degrees of obesity compared to controls, there was no detectable effect on liver steatosis or fibrosis despite the near abrogation of C3ar1 expression. This raises the possibility that the lower levels of hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance previously observed in the whole body C3aR1 KO mice may be secondary to protection from obesity. Protection from diet-induced obesity in whole-body C3aR1 KO mice may be mediated by a non-macrophage cell type, since our macrophage-specific C3aR1 KO mice were not afforded this protection. The C3ar1-expressing cell types that promote obesity and MASLD remains to be determined.

Our laboratory recently reported sex-dependent regulation of thermogenic adipose tissue mediated by adipocyte-derived C3aR1 (Ma et al., 2024). However, no such sexual dimorphism was observed in hepatic expression of key MASH genes in response to GAN diet in our macrophage- or Kupffer-cell-specific C3aR1-deficient mice. Other work has suggested possible compensatory effects from its sister anaphylatoxin receptor C5aR1, with increased cold-induced adipocyte browning and attenuated diet-induced obesity seen in C3aR1/C5aR1 double KO mice (Kong et al., 2023).

The strengths of our study include careful metabolic and transcriptomic phenotyping of cell-type-specific transgenic mice. Some limitations were our use of a single MASLD dietary model and our focus on the C3aR1 pathway. While the GAN diet recapitulates many features of human MASH due to its similarity to Western diet (Vacca et al., 2024), relatively low levels of fibrosis were seen in our study, potentially related to initiating the diet at young age; more rapid fibrosis induction has been seen when GAN diet is initiated at older ages (Li et al., 2023). It is possible that in other models of liver injury that we did not test (e.g. short-term treatment with a hepatotoxin such as carbon tetrachloride; Tsuchida et al., 2018) there may be differences in liver injury in mice lacking C3ar1 in macrophages. However, the GAN diet model has been shown to better parallel the gene expression changes in human MAFLD/MASH (Hansen et al., 2020). Lastly, while C3AR1/C3ar1 expression is very low in non-macrophage cells (Figure 1B), C3aR1 signaling on other hepatic cell types not explored in this study, such as hepatic stellate cells, could mediate the observed effect in the whole-body C3aR1 KO mouse.

Deletion of C3aR1 in macrophages generally, or in liver resident macrophages specifically, had no major effect on systemic glucose homeostasis and hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis in this murine dietary model of MASLD/MASH. The complement system is a complex entity directing an important part of the body’s inflammatory and tissue repair response in MASLD. Further work is needed to elucidate the mechanisms of the role of C3aR1 in the pathogenesis of MASH and cirrhosis.

## Materials and methods

### Animals

C3ar1flox/flox mice were on the C57BL/6 J background as described (Cumpelik et al., 2021). Homozygous Lyz2Cre mice on the C57BL/6 J background (Strain #004781) as well as homozygous Clec4f-Cre mice on the C57BL/6 J background (Strain #003296) were purchased from Jackson Laboratories. C3ar1flox/flox homozygous mice on C57BL/6 J background were used in the experiments as controls from the same backcross generation (Ma et al., 2024). All mice were maintained in plastic cages under a 12 hr/12 hr light/dark cycle at constant temperature (22 °C) with free access to water and food. Mice were fed regular diet containing 4.5%kcal fat PicoLab Rodent diet 20 (LabDiet) or GAN diet containing 40%kcal HFD (mostly palm oil) with 20% fructose and 2% cholesterol (D09100310, Research Diets) for 28–30 weeks. Fat mass and lean mass were determined via noninvasive 3-in-1 body composition analyzer (EchoMRI). Mice were humanely euthanized with CO2 inhalation followed by exsanguination by cardiac puncture. For a typical experiment we expected ~10% loss of animals, a coefficient of variation (CV) of 10% and a treatment/genotype effect of 30–50%. To ensure an adequate statistical power of 0.9 with an alpha value of 0.05, we anticipated 6–12 mice per experimental group for physiology experiments. Key experiments were repeated in at least two independent mouse cohorts.

### Blood chemistry and serum insulin analysis

Mice were fasted overnight (14–16 hr) for glucose tolerance tests and injected intraperitoneally with syringe-filtered D-glucose solution (2 g/kg). For insulin tolerance test, mice were fasted for 6 hr and injected with 0.5 mIU/kg insulin. Blood glucose levels were assayed by commercial glucometer (OneTouch) by tail vein blood samples. Plasma insulin levels were measured from mice fasted for 6 hr. Tail vein blood was collected into lithium heparin-coated tubes, centrifuged at 2000 x g at 4 °C, and plasma insulin levels were determined by ELISA using a standard curve (Mercodia). Serum alanine aminotransferase levels were measured in serum from blood collected via cardiac puncture using a commercially available colorimetric assay (TR71121, Thermo Fisher Scientific).

### Peritoneal macrophage isolation and flow cytometry

Peritoneal macrophages were isolated from as previously described (Zhang et al., 2008). Briefly, mice were euthanized then immediately injected intraperitoneally with 10mL phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.4) at room temperature. After a 3–5min incubation period, peritoneal fluid was removed with sterile needle and syringe and placed on ice. After centrifugation at 300 x g, the pellet was resuspended in PBS containing 2% fetal bovine serum and 0.1% sodium azide. Cells were stained with phycoerythrin-conjugated anti-F4/80 (clone BM8, cat. #123110) and fluorescein isothiocyanate-conjugated anti-CD11b (clone M1/70, cat. #101206) fluorescent antibodies (Biolegend). Stained cells were loaded on MA900 fluorescence-activated cell sorter (Sony), and dual-positive F480+/CD11b+ cells were sorted for subsequent RNA extraction.

### Histological studies

A mid-distal portion of the left liver lobe was fixed with 10% buffered formalin and transferred to 70% ethanol. Samples were embedded in paraffin, sectioned at ~5 μm thickness, and stained with Masson’s trichrome. Slides were imaged using Zeiss Axioscan7 at ×20 magnification. Histologic analyses were performed using ImageJ software (version 1.53t). Lipid droplet area was quantified by subtracting non-droplet area in the green channel from total section area of two to three independent sections. Collagen proportionate area was quantified by measuring total area in the red channel after reducing intensity threshold to 60–70.

### RNA extraction and real-time quantitative PCR analysis

Total RNA from liver tissue lysates was extracted using Trizol reagent (Invitrogen) followed by RNAeasy Mini kit (QIAGEN) as per manufacturer’s protocol. RNA was reverse-transcribed using the High Capacity cDNA RT kit (Thermo Fisher). Quantitative PCR was performed using SYBR Green Master Mix (Quanta) and specific gene primers on QuantStudio6 Flex Real-Time PCR Systems (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using the delta-delta Ct method. Expression levels were normalized to Ribosomal protein S18 (Rps18). Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary file 1.

### Statistical analyses

All statistical analyses were performed with biological replicates using GraphPad Prism10. Unpaired two-tailed Student’s t test with Welch correction for most analyses, with Holm-Šídák correction for multiple comparisons where applicable, and p<0.05 was considered statistically significant.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.100708.3.sa0](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.100708.3.sa0)

This valuable study investigates the role of Complement 3a Receptor 1 (C3aR) in the pathogenesis of Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD) using mouse models with specific target deletions in various cell types. While the general relevance of C3aR in inflammatory contexts has been established before, the authors provide solid evidence here that C3aR does not contribute significantly to MASLD pathogenesis in their models. The work will be of interest to colleagues studying diseases of the liver and the intersection with inflammation.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.100708.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.100708.3.sa2)

Summary:

Homan et al. examined the effect of macrophage- or Kupffer cell-specific C3aR1 KO on MASLD/MASH-related metabolic or liver phenotypes.

Strengths:

Established macrophage- or Kupffer cell-specific C3aR1 KO mice, and showing comparable liver metabolic phenotypes between WT and macrophage-specific C3aR1KO mice in response to normal chow diet or MASH diet feeding.

Weaknesses:

results.result: C3AR1 is expressed primarily in Kupffer cells and macrophages in both human and mouse liver, with minimal expression in hepatocytes and hepatic stellate cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are supported by scRNA-Seq data from Human Protein Atlas (C1), MacParland et al. 2018 (C2-C4), and Tabula Muris (C5). The data consistently show C3AR1/C3ar1 expression is enriched in macrophages/Kupffer cells across species, with visual confirmation in Figures 1A-B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

results.result: CFD and C3AR1 expression are downregulated in human MASLD and MASH liver biopsies compared to healthy and obese controls, with slightly higher levels in MASH versus MASLD.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C17 are supported by bulk transcriptomic analysis from Suppli et al. 2019 cohort shown in Figure 1C. The data show significant downregulation of both genes in MASLD/MASH compared to controls, with statistical significance indicated. The observation of slightly higher levels in MASH vs MASLD (C16-C17) is noted but lacks statistical testing.

results.result: The GAN diet induces MASLD/MASH features in mice including weight gain (primarily fat mass), hepatic steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, fibrosis, and increased expression of inflammatory and fibrotic markers, with attenuated effects in females.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C30 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including body weight curves (Figure 1D), body composition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C), histology (Figures 1E-G), and gene expression data (Figure 1H). The characterization of the MASLD/MASH model is comprehensive with appropriate quantification and statistical analysis.

results.result: Female control mice on GAN diet showed no significant changes in C3ar1 or other gene markers, though nonsignificant trends toward increased inflammation and fibrosis were observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 are supported by gene expression data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D. The lack of statistical significance is appropriately noted, and the observation of nonsignificant trends is a valid descriptive finding, though it limits the strength of conclusions about sex differences.

results.result: Macrophage-specific deletion of C3ar1 reduces hepatic C3ar1 expression by ~88% in both sexes, indicating macrophages account for the vast majority of liver C3ar1 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 and C187 are supported by gene expression data from peritoneal macrophages (Figure 2A) and whole liver tissue (Figure 2B) in C3aR1-MφKO mice. The ~88% reduction provides strong quantitative evidence that macrophages are the predominant source of hepatic C3ar1 expression.

results.result: Macrophage-specific C3aR1 deletion does not affect body weight gain, body composition, glucose tolerance, insulin sensitivity, or serum ALT levels in mice on GAN diet.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C44, C83-C84, and C100 are supported by comprehensive metabolic phenotyping data shown in Figures 2C-E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C. Multiple independent measures of metabolism show no significant differences between control and C3aR1-MφKO mice, providing strong evidence for lack of metabolic effects.

results.result: Macrophage-specific C3aR1 deletion does not affect liver mass, hepatic steatosis, or liver fibrosis in mice on GAN or regular diet.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C51, C85-C86 are supported by liver mass measurements (Figure 2F), histological analysis (Figure 2G), and quantitative image analysis of lipid droplets and collagen (Figures 2H-I). The lack of differences in multiple independent measures of liver pathology provides strong evidence.

results.result: Despite marked reduction in C3ar1 expression, C3aR1-MφKO mice show no detectable changes in hepatic gene expression markers of fibrosis, inflammation, or lipid handling on either GAN or regular diet in both sexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C62 are supported by comprehensive gene expression analysis shown in Figures 2J-K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D. The lack of transcriptional changes despite successful knockout provides strong negative evidence that macrophage C3aR1 does not regulate these pathways in this model.

results.result: Kupffer cell-specific C3aR1 deletion does not affect body weight gain, body composition, glucose homeostasis, or liver mass in mice on GAN diet.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67, C87-C88 are supported by body weight curves (Figure 3A), body composition (Figure 3B), glucose tolerance tests (Figure 3C), and liver mass measurements (Figure 3D). The data parallel the macrophage-specific knockout findings, strengthening the conclusion that C3aR1 in these cell types is not required for metabolic phenotypes.

results.result: Kupffer cell-specific C3aR1 deletion does not affect hepatic steatosis or fibrosis as measured by histology and quantitative image analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70, C89-C90 are supported by histological images (Figure 3E) and quantitative analysis of lipid droplets (Figure 3F) and collagen (Figure 3G). The findings are consistent with the macrophage-specific knockout results, providing convergent evidence.

results.result: C3ar1 expression is reduced by 73-90% in liver tissue of C3aR1-KpKO mice, indicating Kupffer cells account for ~80% of hepatic C3ar1 expression, but no changes in inflammatory, fibrotic, or lipid handling gene markers are observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76 are supported by gene expression data in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A. The quantification of C3ar1 reduction provides evidence for the cellular source, while the lack of downstream gene expression changes parallels the macrophage-specific knockout findings.

results.result: Macrophage and Kupffer cell expression of C3ar1 does not impact body weight, glucose homeostasis, or histologic/transcriptomic features of MASLD/MASH in the murine GAN diet model.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C82 and C103-C127 represent summary statements of the experimental findings from both knockout models. These are well-supported by the comprehensive data from Figures 2 and 3, showing consistent lack of phenotypic differences across multiple metabolic and hepatic parameters in both C3aR1-MφKO and C3aR1-KpKO mice.

results.result: The findings in macrophage/Kupffer cell-specific C3aR1 KO mice contrast with whole-body C3aR1 KO mice, suggesting protection from obesity and hepatic steatosis in whole-body KO may be mediated by non-macrophage cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C99 and C101 appropriately compare current findings with Mamane et al. 2009. The contrast between cell-type-specific and whole-body knockouts is well-documented, and the speculation about non-macrophage cell types (C99, C101) is reasonable given the data, though it remains speculative and requires future investigation.

results.result: Kupffer cells are the predominant liver cell type expressing C3ar1.
results.evaluation: Claim C128 is supported by the ~73-90% reduction in hepatic C3ar1 expression in Kupffer cell-specific knockout mice (Figures 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), combined with scRNA-Seq data showing predominant expression in Kupffer cells (Figures 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

results.result: C3AR1/C3ar1 expression is very low in non-macrophage liver cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by scRNA-Seq data in Figure 1B showing minimal-to-undetectable expression in hepatocytes and hepatic stellate cells. This finding is important for interpreting the cell-type-specific knockout results.

results.result: No sexual dimorphism was observed in hepatic expression of key MASH genes in response to GAN diet in macrophage- or Kupffer cell-specific C3aR1-deficient mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C175 is supported by gene expression data in Figures 2J-K and 3H showing similar patterns in males and females. This contrasts with prior work on adipocyte C3aR1 (C174), suggesting tissue-specific differences in sex-dependent regulation.

results.result: Relatively low levels of fibrosis were observed in the study, potentially related to initiating the GAN diet at young age.
results.evaluation: Claim C188 is supported by the observation of modest fibrosis levels in the histological data (Figures 1G, 2I, 3G) and comparison with Li et al. 2023. This is an important limitation of the study that may affect interpretation of fibrosis-related findings.

results.result: The GAN diet model has macronutrient similarities to Western diet and produces similar histologic and transcriptomic changes to human MASLD/MASH.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C173, C179, and C186 are supported by citations to Boland et al. 2019, Hansen et al. 2020, and Vacca et al. 2024. The diet composition is clearly specified (C186), and the model's relevance to human disease is established by prior literature, though the authors acknowledge limitations regarding fibrosis levels (C188).

results.result: The mouse models used appropriate genetic backgrounds and controls, with C3ar1flox/flox mice on C57BL/6J background crossed to Lyz2Cre or Clec4f-Cre mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C182-C185 describe the mouse strains and experimental design. These are supported by citations and clear methodological descriptions. The use of littermate controls from the same backcross generation (C185) is appropriate for genetic studies.

results.result: Compensatory effects from C5aR1 may occur in C3aR1 knockout mice, as C3aR1/C5aR1 double KO mice show enhanced metabolic phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C176-C178 cite Kong et al. 2023 regarding potential compensatory mechanisms. This is relevant context for interpreting the lack of phenotype in the current study, though it remains speculative whether such compensation occurs in the macrophage/Kupffer cell-specific models tested here.

results.result: C3AR1 is broadly expressed throughout the human body with enrichment in immune tissues, and in both human and mouse liver, C3AR1/C3ar1 is expressed primarily in Kupffer cells and macrophages, with minimal-to-undetectable expression in hepatocytes or hepatic stellate cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these expression pattern claims. The editor's summary states the authors 'provide solid evidence' and reviewers accepted the establishment of the model system, implicitly affirming the foundational expression data shown in Figures 1A-B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

results.result: In human liver biopsies, CFD and C3AR1 are unchanged in obese subjects without MASLD compared to healthy controls, but both are significantly downregulated in MASLD and MASH patients compared to both healthy controls and obese subjects without MASLD, with slightly higher levels in MASH compared to MASLD only.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question these human transcriptomic findings from the Suppli et al., 2019 cohort shown in Figure 1C. The editor noted the work is 'valuable' and reviewers accepted the human data context without critique.

results.result: Male C3ar1flox/flox control mice on GAN diet for 28 weeks gained body weight primarily as fat mass and developed histologic signs of MASLD including hepatic steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, and nearly doubled liver fibrosis, with robustly increased hepatic C3ar1, Cfd, and markers of macrophage infiltration, inflammation, and fibrosis indicating progression to fibrotic MASH; female mice showed attenuated weight gain and nonsignificant trends in gene expression changes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the GAN diet model characterization. The editor stated the authors 'provide solid evidence' and reviewers acknowledged the model was established, accepting the baseline phenotypic characterization shown in Figures 1D-H and supplementary figures.

results.result: C3ar1 expression was reduced by ~88% in liver tissue of both male and female C3aR1-MφKO mice, indicating that macrophages account for the vast majority of hepatic C3ar1 expression, with successful deletion confirmed by quantitative RT-PCR of isolated peritoneal macrophages.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the establishment of the macrophage-specific knockout model. One reviewer explicitly noted as a strength: 'Established macrophage- or Kupffer cell-specific C3aR1 KO mice,' affirming the technical validity shown in Figures 2A-B.

results.result: Deletion of C3aR1 in macrophages (C3aR1-MφKO mice) did not affect weight gain, body composition, glucose tolerance, insulin sensitivity, HOMA-IR, serum ALT levels, or liver mass in mice on GAN diet compared to controls, indicating macrophage C3aR1 does not impact systemic metabolic parameters or glucose homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these metabolic phenotype findings. One reviewer noted as a strength: 'showing comparable liver metabolic phenotypes between WT and macrophage-specific C3aR1KO mice,' affirming the lack of differences shown in Figures 2C-F and supplementary figures.

results.result: Male C3aR1-MφKO mice on GAN diet developed similar histologic appearance, lipid droplet area, and collagen area compared to controls, with no detectable gene expression changes in markers of fibrosis, inflammation, or lipid handling on either GAN or regular diet in both male and female mice, indicating macrophage C3aR1 deletion has no significant effect on hepatic steatosis, inflammation, or fibrosis.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accepted the overall conclusion of no effect, one reviewer identified a critical weakness: 'Insufficient data showing the effects of C3aR1KO on liver macrophage phenotypes, such as hepatic macrophage profiles, macrophage activation status, etc, which are important for the development of liver steatosis and fibrosis.' This indicates the evidence is incomplete despite the negative findings shown in Figures 2G-K.

results.result: Body weight gain, body composition, glucose homeostasis during glucose tolerance test, and liver mass were similar between control and C3aR1-KpKO (Kupffer cell-specific knockout) mice on GAN diet for both male and female mice, indicating Kupffer cell C3aR1 does not impact these metabolic parameters.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as part of the overall negative result. The editor stated the authors 'provide solid evidence' that C3aR does not contribute significantly to MASLD pathogenesis, encompassing these metabolic measurements shown in Figures 3A-D.

results.result: Liver sections from C3aR1-KpKO mice appeared qualitatively similar to controls by histology, with similar levels of hepatic steatosis measured by lipid droplet area and no significant difference in liver fibrosis measured by collagen area; C3ar1 expression was reduced by 73-90% in liver tissue, indicating Kupffer cells account for ~80% of hepatic C3ar1 expression, yet there were no significant differences in expression of inflammatory, fibrotic, or lipid handling gene markers.
results.evaluation: Similar to the macrophage knockout, reviewers accepted the negative findings but one reviewer noted the critical weakness: 'Insufficient data showing the effects of C3aR1KO on liver macrophage phenotypes, such as hepatic macrophage profiles, macrophage activation status.' This limitation applies equally to the Kupffer cell-specific model shown in Figures 3E-H, indicating incomplete mechanistic characterization.

results.result: Overall, macrophage or Kupffer cell expression of C3ar1 does not impact body weight gain or histologic/transcriptomic features of MASLD/MASH in the murine dietary model; these findings contrast with prior observations in whole-body C3aR1 KO mice which are protected from diet-induced obesity, suggesting protection may be mediated by a non-macrophage cell type, possibly hepatic stellate cells despite very low C3AR1 expression in non-macrophage cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this overall conclusion. The editor's assessment states the authors 'provide solid evidence here that C3aR does not contribute significantly to MASLD pathogenesis in their models,' and one reviewer noted the work 'rule[s] out the role of Complement 3a Receptor 1 in the pathogenesis of disease.' The comparison with whole-body knockout and speculation about other cell types is appropriately framed.

results.result: Whole-body C3aR1 KO mice (from prior literature) are protected from diet-induced obesity, have improved glucose tolerance, exhibit decreased hepatic steatosis and inflammation, decreased macrophage infiltration and activation in adipose tissue, and show blunted activation of hepatic stellate cells by bone-marrow-derived macrophages in a model of fibrosing steatohepatitis.
results.evaluation: These are cited findings from prior literature (Mamane et al., 2009; Han et al., 2019) used for comparison. Reviewers did not challenge these citations, and they provide important context for interpreting the current negative findings in cell-type-specific models.

results.result: Background and methodological context claims including: MASLD epidemiology, complement system biology, prior adipsin/CFD findings, GAN diet characteristics, mouse strain information, and study limitations such as relatively low fibrosis levels potentially related to diet initiation age.
results.evaluation: These background, methodological, and contextual claims were not challenged by reviewers. They provide necessary scientific context and methodological transparency. The acknowledgment of study limitations (e.g., relatively low fibrosis) demonstrates appropriate scientific rigor.

comparisons.comparison: Both support C3AR1/C3ar1 expression patterns in macrophages/Kupffer cells (C1-C5). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of scRNA-Seq data sources, while peer reviewers implicitly accepted these foundational expression data without challenge. Peer result also includes C115, C116, C128 which relate to expression patterns.

Strong agreement on human transcriptomic data showing C3/C3AR1 downregulation in MASLD/MASH (C6-C17). Both evaluations support these findings from Suppli et al. 2019 cohort. OpenEval notes lack of statistical testing for MASH vs MASLD comparison; peer reviewers accepted without critique.

Both support GAN diet model characterization (C18-C34). OpenEval provides comprehensive assessment of body weight, composition, histology, and gene expression. Peer reviewers accepted model establishment as 'solid evidence' without challenging the characterization data.

Both support establishment of macrophage-specific knockout model (C35-C37, C187). OpenEval emphasizes the ~88% reduction in hepatic C3ar1 as evidence of macrophages as predominant source. Peer reviewers explicitly noted this as a strength. Peer result also includes C52 (gene expression).

Both support lack of metabolic phenotype differences in C3aR1-MφKO mice (C38-C44, C83-C84, C100). OpenEval details comprehensive metabolic phenotyping; peer reviewers accepted these findings as strength showing 'comparable liver metabolic phenotypes.' Peer result extends to C45-C46 and C103, C118.
